idiom_name: ARC: strong/weak/unowned references with deinit (class instances)
implementation_notes: Swift class instances already are smart pointers: ARC tracks strong references and releases the instance when the last one is broken, so an ordinary assignment is an owning handle. The ownership kinds are expressed by language keywords - weak is a zeroing non-owning reference (an Optional that becomes nil after release) and unowned a non-optional non-owning reference that assumes the referent outlives it - and deinit performs deterministic release when the count reaches zero. What replaces the classic structure: these reference kinds, used deliberately to break the strong cycles that ARC (like every refcounting scheme) leaks, plus withExtendedLifetime where the optimizer must be told a borrow keeps the object alive. Value types (struct and enum) are copied and never need any of this.
pitfalls: weak must be a var of an Optional class type (never let), and strong closure captures are the other common cycle - capture [weak self] in escaping closures.
unowned is unchecked: using it after the referent dies traps in debug or is undefined in unchecked builds; prefer weak for delegate-style edges and unowned only where the lifetime ordering is proven.
ARC leaks strong reference cycles built from two strong references; the design must name which edge is weak or unowned.
deinit timing is only guaranteed for acyclic objects; cleanup that 'will happen in deinit' needs a proven acyclic graph, otherwise it must be explicit.
